summary: Gives a scenario for using the Network Journal: users mail messages or whole files to the NIC using SNDMSG or their site's mail, and the NIC converts them to NLS files, journalizes them and sends them to recipients.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 629 shows how to send messages and files through the Network Journal and how to retrieve journal files later. It gives examples for SNDMSG, Telnet, FTP and other local mail systems.

subtitle: Examples for sending and retrieving messages through the Network Journal.

tldr.problem: Network Journal users needed practical instructions for submitting messages or files and retrieving journalized files.
tldr.mechanism: Users address mail to NIC with a slash-separated sender and recipient identifier; the NIC converts it to an NLS file and distributes it. Longer items can be retrieved later by FTP using their citation.
tldr.outcome: The RFC provides example workflows for SNDMSG, FTP, Telnet and other local mail systems.

today: RFC 629 is a procedural guide to sending and retrieving items through the Network Journal.

sections.title: How the Network Journal Handles Mail
sections.content:
Users could send messages or whole files to individuals or groups through the Network Journal using SNDMSG or their local mail system. At the NIC, mail was converted to NLS files, journalized and sent to the specified recipients. Short messages could arrive as messages; longer ones could arrive as citations to files that users could retrieve immediately or later with FTP.

Sending mail to NIC with a slash in the user-name field invoked the Network Journal.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC converted submitted mail into NLS files, recorded them in the Journal and sent them to the named recipients. Longer items could be retrieved later using a citation.

sections.title: Sending Messages and Files
sections.content:
The SNDMSG example uses a user field containing a sender NIC identifier, a slash and recipient identifier or identifiers, followed by @NIC. A group identifier could stand for a group. The sender could add ordinary network addresses after a comma to send the same mail through regular mail as well. The example also shows inserting a sequential file into a message with ^B.

For Telnet or FTP, the RFC shows using the NIC's mail service and ending message text with a line containing only a period. Other local mail systems should use NIC as the host and the sender/recipient NIC identifiers in the user name.
sections.plainLanguage: Address the Journal with the sender's NIC identifier, a slash and the recipient identifiers. The examples show how to include a file and how users of Telnet or FTP can enter message text.

sections.title: Retrieving a Journal File
sections.content: When a recipient receives a citation such as <GJOURNAL>21695, the RFC shows replacing the citation number in the file name and retrieving the NLS file from NIC with FTP. The example connects to NIC, logs in as ANONYMOUS with NIC as the password, issues a GET for the journal file and disconnects after transfer.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the citation as the journal file number in an FTP request to NIC. The example retrieves the file and saves it locally.
